Are you sure you're up for the five year old version? Basically, we have the electoral college because you can vote.

There are not two votes by the Electoral College.

On the November election day, the popular vote in each state determines which Electors each state will send to the Electoral College. The Electors are NOT voting on that day. You will hear all the news reports saying things like "Trump has this many electors, Hillary has this many electors." This is not indicating that those Electors are voting in the EC at that time. What the news reports are actually counting is how many Electors will be sent to the Electoral College to do the EC vote in December.

So the popular vote in November selects the Electors. The Electoral College vote in December selects the president.

But I hasten to add that the Electors vote primarily based on the candidate that they have "pledged" to support. So, for example, when the people of North Dakota voted to support Trump, what was actually being chosen was to send three Electors that support Trump to the College. If Hillary had won in ND, then three Electors that supported her would have gone to the College instead.

So the people's vote in each state does have a direct consequence on the election of the president. Just because it is a two stage event doesn't mean that the individual vote doesn't count.

It's also important to note that for each state's electors differing rules can apply. Usually each state has their electors vote for whoever one the popular vote in their state but I believe 1 or 2 states actually use proportional voting for distributing their electors.

I think proportional is probably the way to go but we work with the system we have in place at the time of election.

A state's decision to use proportional representation in the Electoral College probably sounds most attractive if you look at the election as a strictly national affair. However, if you look at the issue from the perspective of each individual state, the problem looks a little different.

Since I used North Dakota as an example above, I'll continue to do so. If ND used proportional representation among it's Electors, it could well be sending 2 Electors for Trump and 1 Elector for Clinton in this election. Now, North Dakota want's to select the national executive that will have the best impact for North Dakota. That's the reason that states have representation in the college. By choosing proportional representation ND is only casting +1 votes for a candidate (on balance) instead of +3 votes.

So in that scenario, North Dakota would be voluntarily cutting their influence in the election of a president by 66%. Why would a state want to give up it's influence? Wouldn't a state want to preserve as much influence as possible?

This is the line of reasoning that has brought every state to employ a winner take all approach to the selection of Electors, at one point in time or another. Two states have since switched to using a non-take-all method. (They don't exactly use a "proportional" method, but we'll take a few liberties with the term.)
